rules.statement: Do not write audit or telemetry records to a database inline on the request path; add them to a bounded in-memory queue and have a hosted background service write the queue in batches.
rules.why: An inline write adds a database round trip to every audited operation, and a failed audit write would fail the operation.
rules.check: Look for an event or audit handler that calls a store, DbContext or SaveChanges directly while the request is being handled, rather than enqueuing the record for a background flush.

rules.statement: When a bounded in-memory queue drops items because it is full, count the drops and log the count once per flush interval, not once per dropped item.
rules.why: Dropped records have to be visible to operators, and logging each drop would flood the log just when the system is overloaded.
rules.check: Look for a bounded queue or channel whose full-queue path drops items silently, or logs on every dropped item instead of reporting an aggregated count during the periodic flush.

rules.statement: A background batch writer keeps a failed batch and writes it first on the next flush, and the store makes the write idempotent with a unique index on the record's identifier, skipping identifiers it already holds.
rules.why: If a save commits but still reports a failure, the retried batch must not insert the same records twice.
rules.check: Look for a batch flush that discards a batch when the write fails, or that retries it without a unique key and a skip of existing ids, which would create duplicates.

rules.statement: A hosted service that flushes buffered data when the host stops must run that final flush exactly once, with concurrent or repeated StopAsync calls sharing the same flush.
rules.why: The host may stop a service twice, and the held records should be written only once.
rules.check: Look for StopAsync implementations whose final flush runs again on every call, or that race with each other, instead of sharing one cached task or flush guarded by a once-only check.

rules.statement: Each lookup index starts with the column the query filters on and then the time column the query sorts by.
rules.why: Lookups filter on one field over a time range and sort by time, so the index has to match that access pattern.
rules.check: Look for new indexes on time-ordered records that leave out the time column or put it before the filter column.

rules.statement: When an indexed column is denormalized from a full JSON document and the value is longer than the column, store null for an optional field and the leading characters for a required one, and keep the full value in the JSON document.
rules.why: A value that is too long must not fail the write, and the full JSON stays the authoritative record.
rules.check: Look for writes into length-limited indexed columns that can throw or lose the only copy of a value that is too long, or that cut off optional values instead of storing null.

rules.statement: Use keyset paging ordered by the sort key plus a unique surrogate identifier as tie-breaker, backed by an index on those columns, and have the opaque cursor carry the last item's sort key and identifier.
rules.why: Several records can share the same timestamp, so the identifier is needed for a stable order with no duplicates or gaps across pages.
rules.check: Look for paged queries that sort only by a timestamp that is not unique, use offset paging, or have cursors that leave out the tie-breaking identifier.

rules.statement: API time-range filters treat the start time as inclusive and the end time as exclusive.
rules.why: Half-open ranges match the convention the API follows, and adjacent ranges then neither overlap nor leave gaps.
rules.check: Look for range filters that use <= on the end time, or > on the start time.

rules.statement: When querying records that are not tenant-scoped but carry a tenant column, put the addressed tenant in the query explicitly every time, and never list records that have no tenant.
rules.why: These records are not covered by automatic tenant scoping, so leaving out the tenant criterion would expose other tenants' records.
rules.check: Look for tenant-addressed endpoints that query non-tenant-scoped tables without an explicit TenantId == tenantId predicate.

rules.statement: Bind options for intervals, capacities and retentions strictly from configuration and validate them when the host starts, including an Enabled switch where the feature can be turned off.
rules.why: Bad intervals or retention values should fail at startup, not at runtime.
rules.check: Look for new options classes that are not registered with ValidateOnStart and validation, or that are bound without strict binding.
